AM8N-01.note: 32 = 2^5 (added exponents 3+2 then x2 wrongly), 256 = 2^8, 66 = 64+2. All reachable from a named slip.

AM8N-02.solved: x - 3 = 8 or x - 3 = -8, so x = 11 or x = -5; greatest is 11.
AM8N-02.note: -5 is the other root, 5 drops the sign case, 24 = 8x3 is the weakest option.

AM8N-03.solved: sqrt(50) = 5 sqrt(2), sqrt(18) = 3 sqrt(2); sum = 8 sqrt(2), so k = 8.
AM8N-03.note: 68 = 50+18 under the sqrt (adds radicands), 15 = 5x3 (multiplies coefficients). 4 is weak - no wrong path I can name produces it.

AM8N-04.note: 47 = 7 + 10x4 is the off-by-one, which is the whole point of the item. 36 = 9x4 drops the first term.

AM8N-05.solved: r^2 = 27/12 = 9/4, r = 3/2 (positive terms), so a3 = 12(3/2) = 18. Equivalently the geometric mean sqrt(12x27) = sqrt(324) = 18.
AM8N-05.note: 19.5 is the arithmetic mean of 12 and 27 - the exact error the item is built on. 'all positive terms' is load-bearing and correctly stated (it kills r = -3/2).

AM8N-07.solved: Leading digit cannot be 0: 3 choices; then 3 remaining for the tens; then 2 for the units. 3 x 3 x 2 = 18.
AM8N-07.note: 24 = 4P3 is the no-leading-zero miss and is the strongest distractor in the batch. This is my closest medium/hard call - see the report. The phrase '3-digit integers' does state the constraint, so the student is executing the stem, not noticing past it.

AM8N-08.solved: Row 1 of A dotted with column 2 of B: (3)(0) + (-1)(7) = -7.
AM8N-08.note: 0 comes from multiplying entrywise (3x0); 17 = (3)(5)+(2)... i.e. a row/column mix-up; -5 is a sign/position slip. Matrix given in prose rather than a graphic, which is fine but makes the row/column reference the only thing a careless reader can drop.

AM8N-09.note: Option set is exactly {1, i, -1, -i}, so a blind solver gets 25% and nothing more - clean by construction. Every distractor is a different residue.

AM8N-10.solved: Multiples of 4 below 300: 4..296, that is 74. Multiples of both 4 and 6 are multiples of lcm = 12: 12..288, that is 24. 74 - 24 = 50.
AM8N-10.note: 74 is the 'forgot to subtract' option and 99 counts multiples of 3. The lcm step is a taught habit rather than a noticing, which is why I did not grade this hard.

AM8N-11.note: 12 = 16 x 3/4, 64 = 4^3 (fourth root confused with square root), 2 = 16^(1/4) alone.

AM8N-12.note: 15 = 3x5 (no squaring), 225 = (3x5)^2 (squares the whole thing including the 5 twice). 8 is weak.

AM8N-13.solved: First sequence: 4, 11, 18, 25, 32, 39. Second: 9, 14, 19, 24, 29, 34, 39. First common term is 39. (4 satisfies both congruences - 4 mod 7 and 4 mod 5 - but the second sequence BEGINS at 9, so 4 is not a term of it.)
AM8N-13.note: HARD. Option D = 4 is the designed trap for a student who solves by congruences and never checks that the value lies at or after each sequence's first term. 44 = 39 + 5 catches a student who lands on 39 in one sequence and steps the wrong one. I considered exclusive:false on the grounds that someone might read a sequence as extending backwards, but 'begins 9, 14, 19, 24' fixes the first term, so 4 is not defensible.

AM8N-14.solved: Scaling every entry of an n x n matrix by k multiplies the determinant by k^n. Here n = 2, so det(3A) = 3^2 x 6 = 54. (Check directly: det[[3a,3b],[3c,3d]] = 9(ad-bc).)
AM8N-14.note: HARD, but by a different mechanism than 13/22/27: this is knowledge-gated rather than two ideas interacting. 18 = 3x6 is the answer for every student who has not met the k^n rule, and nothing in the stem hints the factor is 9 rather than 3. 27 = 3^3 catches the student who has the rule but the wrong n. Graders who require 'two ideas interact' rather than 'must notice something unstated' may downgrade this to medium; I kept it hard because the unstated thing is the entire item.

AM8N-15.solved: 84 = 2^2 x 3 x 7, 126 = 2 x 3^2 x 7; common factors 2 x 3 x 7 = 42.
AM8N-15.note: 252 is the lcm (the standard GCF/LCM swap), 6 and 14 are partial common factors.

AM8N-16.solved: n = 12q + 5, so n^2 = 144q^2 + 120q + 25; the first two terms are multiples of 12 and 25 = 2(12) + 1, so the remainder is 1.
AM8N-16.note: 25 and 13 are both 'forgot to reduce' options, and 13 is the sharper of the two because it is one reduction short. I graded medium rather than hard: 'the remainder when n^2 is divided by 12' states the reduction, so a student who finishes the sentence they were given reduces 25.

AM8N-17.note: 336 = P(8,3) is the permutation/combination confusion and is the reason this is medium rather than easy. 512 = 8^3, 24 = 8x3.

AM8N-18.note: 33 = 29 + 4 (sign error on i^2), 5 = k rather than k^2 (the stem asks for k^2, so this is the read-the-question distractor). 'k positive real' is present and does real work.

AM8N-19.note: 192 = 6 x 2^5 is the off-by-one; 14 = 6 + 4x2 treats it as arithmetic. Near-twin of AM8N-04 in structure (same off-by-one architecture, geometric instead of arithmetic).

AM8N-20.solved: Equal distances means x is the midpoint of 3 and -7: x = (3 + (-7))/2 = -2. Check: |-2-3| = 5 = |-2+7|.
AM8N-20.note: -5 and 5 come from dropping a sign when squaring or from solving x-3 = x+7 badly; 10 = 3+7. No second root exists (the x-3 = x+7 branch is empty), which a student may not realise, but that does not create a second defensible option.

AM8N-21.solved: (2 x 3)(3 x 4) gives a 2 x 4 product: rows from A, columns from B.
AM8N-21.note: '4 rows and 2 columns' is the transposed answer, '2 rows and 3 columns' just echoes A. Pure definition recall.

AM8N-22.solved: The 40 multiples run 3 to 120. One-digit: 3, 6, 9 = 3 numbers. Two-digit: 12 to 99 = (99-12)/3 + 1 = 30 numbers. Three-digit: 102 to 120 = 7 numbers. (3+30+7 = 40, checks.) Digits = 3(1) + 30(2) + 7(3) = 3 + 60 + 21 = 84.
AM8N-22.note: HARD, and the cleanest hard item in the batch. Nothing in the stem mentions digit length changing; the student has to invent the bucketing and then count each bucket correctly. 120 is the last number (and also 40x3, doubly attractive), 80 = 40x2 assumes every number is two digits, 40 counts the numbers not the digits.

AM8N-23.solved: First multiple above 20 is 21, last below 150 is 147: (147-21)/7 + 1 = 19.
AM8N-23.note: 18 is the off-by-one from omitting the +1, 21 and 147 are the endpoints themselves. Neither 20 nor 150 is a multiple of 7, so 'between' is unambiguous here - worth saying because the same stem with different bounds would not be.

AM8N-24.note: 2 + 6i is the numerator before dividing by 2 - the single most common real slip on this item type, and it is present. 1 - 3i is the conjugate sign error.

AM8N-25.note: 3/5 is the reciprocal (inverts the common-base step), 4 = 32-8/... loosely 'difference' reasoning, 24 = 8x3. The reciprocal option is the one that does the work.

AM8N-26.note: -2 = -7+5 (added instead of subtracted), 35 = 7x5, 7 is a bare endpoint. Easiest item in the batch.

AM8N-27.solved: n = 21m. n^2 = 441 m^2 and 441 is odd, so 8 must divide m^2. m^2 divisible by 8 forces m divisible by 4 (m = 2 gives m^2 = 4, not enough). Least m = 4, so n = 84. Check: 84^2 = 7056 = 8 x 882.
AM8N-27.note: HARD. The unstated step is that 8 | n^2 requires 4 | n, not 2 | n - 42 is a multiple of 21 and even, and 42^2 = 1764 is NOT divisible by 8, so option B punishes exactly the student who stops at 'even'. 56 is even and divisible by 8-friendly factors but is not a multiple of 21; 21 ignores the second condition. Best-constructed option set in the batch.

AM8N-28.note: 20 is the all-red count (the complement itself, i.e. subtracted the wrong way or forgot the last step) and 60 = C(4,1)C(6,2) is exactly-one-blue. Both are real wrong paths. Graded medium, not hard: 'at least 1' is the standard trigger for the complement habit, so this is a rehearsed move rather than a noticing.
